opening.headline: Explains how to control model invocation permissions in Snowflake and how to use versions and aliases in the Model Registry.
body: In an environment where AI functions are called within SQL, who is allowed to make the call directly relates to cost and data exposure issues. By default, all users of the account can make the call.

In this class, we examine the configuration of AI function call permissions, model access allowance lists and RBAC, as well as the object structure of the Model Registry. We then discuss examples of allowing function calls only to specific teams and examples of specifying operational versions.

As of October 2026: The allowlist is scheduled for deprecation. The following examples combining "All" and RBAC are previous audit cases applicable to accounts that were previously governed by the existing allowlist. This does not apply to accounts where the RBAC-specific actions from the July 2026 change bundle are activated.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain Snowflake's model access control and version/alias in the Model Registry
AI function permissions and model access allowance scopes can be distinguished.

screens.title: Model call permissions in Snowflake — who holds them?
screens.lead:
First, let's examine how model invocations are handled in Snowflake. Consider the scene and think about who is authorized to make such calls.

As of 2026-10: The allowance list will be deprecated. The "All" and RBAC OR combination examples below reflect the prior audit practices for accounts that previously used the allowance list. This does not apply to accounts where RBAC-exclusive behavior has been activated in the 2026_07 change bundle.

paragraphs: In Snowflake, you can call AI functions within SQL to use large language models (LLMs). Since each query line corresponds to a model call, the question of who can invoke this function directly becomes the issue of controlling cost and data exposure.

However, if you leave the default settings unchanged, all users of the account can call AI functions. This is precisely why the marketing team is using the summarization function without being explicitly granted permissions.

One more point of distinction is that the device determining which model can be called is different from the device determining which users can access my model registered in the model registry. Although both are treated as permission objects, their targets differ.
In this class, we explain Snowflake's model access control and model registry versioning and aliases, and we distinguish between AI function permissions and model access allowance scopes.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: To prevent a model call, should we close function permissions or close the model list? Answer this question when you finish the lesson.

visual.alt: Flow diagram of default authorization where calling permissions to all roles are inherited from the PUBLIC role.
labels: Default value: callable by all users

screens.outro: Having verified the baseline state, let's consider it in relation to other platforms.

screens.title: How does another platform and its authorization model differ?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: What's the difference between blocking model calls via API key and blocking them based on role and permissions?
items.answer: The API key method allows anyone with a key to make calls, and control breaks down when keys are compromised. The role-based method determines call eligibility based on user identity, making it easier to manage changes due to employee departures or transfers. Snowflake uses roles and permissions as its foundational model.

items.prompt: What advantages and disadvantages would there be in limiting the model list to an allowed list?
items.answer: The advantage is that the configuration is simple and applies uniformly across the entire account. The drawback is that it is difficult to set different allowances for different teams. Therefore, when more granular control is needed, a role-based permission approach becomes necessary.

items.prompt: Have you seen elsewhere the concept of attaching a label to a model version to indicate the operating version?
items.answer: This is a concept similar to aliases used in other registries. Snowflake's Model Registry also has a similar concept, allowing you to switch operational versions without changing the code. This is confirmed later using the ALTER MODEL statement.

screens.outro: After comparing, let's first look at how AI function call permissions are configured.

screens.title: Cortex AI Function Permissions: Account Permissions and Database Roles
screens.lead: Read the following SQL from top to bottom, and verify against the right-hand description whether each line's meaning matches or diverges.

notes.note: The USE AI FUNCTIONS is initially granted to PUBLIC, allowing all users to use it. When revoked from PUBLIC, the default grant is removed. This action is performed by ACCOUNTADMIN. If not revoked, subsequent grants will not have restricted effects.

At the function level, individual permissions such as USE AI FUNCTION AI_COMPLETE can be granted. These individual permissions operate in an OR relationship with broader permissions, meaning that a role with broad permissions can invoke all functions without requiring individual permissions.

To use AI functions, you need both account permissions and either the CORTEX_USER or AI_FUNCTIONS_USER database roles. If either of these is missing, the call will be rejected. With only account permissions, you can only use functions like AI_AGG and AI_SUMMARIZE_AGG.
A role must be assigned to a user in order for an actual user to be able to make the call. If a role is created but not assigned to a user, no one will be able to make the call.

screens.outro: Since we have read the function call permission, let's look at how to determine which model can be called.

screens.title: Model Access Allowance List: Allowance List and RBAC
screens.lead: See how the behavior works when used together with two methods for restricting model access by selecting each tab.

tabs.label: Allowlist
tabs.body:
As of October 2026, CORTEX_MODELS_ALLOWLIST is in the process of being deprecated. No new model list can be assigned after August 2026, and the only allowed change is to set it to 'None'. This is being considered as part of the review for transitioning existing configurations to RBAC. 

```sql
ALTER ACCOUNT SET CORTEX_MODELS_ALLOWLIST = 'None';
```

tabs.label: RBAC
tabs.body:
Role-based access grants permissions to objects representing models on a per-role basis, enabling more granular control. The Cortex model is not itself a Snowflake object, but objects representing models are created and updated daily within the `SNOWFLAKE.MODELS` schema. Application roles are assigned to specific or all models based on roles. 

```sql
GRANT APPLICATION ROLE SNOWFLAKE."CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-LLAMA3.1-70B" TO ROLE my_role;
```

tabs.label: When used together
tabs.body: Using both methods together allows access if either one is permitted—effectively combined with an OR operation. Therefore, if you want to control access solely using RBAC, you should set the allow list to `None`. When the allow list is set to `All`, roles blocked by RBAC can still be accessed due to the allow list. First, you must verify the existing account's allow list and whether the change bundle has been applied.

tabs.label: When verifying
tabs.body: ACCOUNTADMIN has access to all models, regardless of allowed lists or RBAC configurations. Users with the ACCOUNTADMIN secondary role are subject to the same restriction. To verify that restrictions are working as intended, test using a role other than ACCOUNTADMIN, and ensure the secondary role is disabled for `USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE`.

screens.outro: Having distinguished between call permissions and allowed scopes, I will now examine the Model Registry to define access for the models I have registered.

screens.title: Model Registry: version, base version, alias, ALTER MODEL
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through and examine the object structure, permissions, and alias designation methods of the Model Registry one step at a time.

steps.title: Schema-level objects
steps.body: The Model Registry stores models as schema-level objects and manages model versions, metrics, and metadata. Access is controlled via RBAC. Unlike the Cortex model previously discussed, this model is a actual Snowflake object.

steps.title: Create and write permissions
steps.body: To create a model, you must own the schema or have `CREATE MODEL` privileges. To use a model, you must own the model or have `USAGE` or `READ` privileges.

steps.title: USAGE and READ
steps.body: `USAGE` puts the model in a state where internal details are not visible and is used for warehouse inference. `READ` allows viewing comments, tags, and indicators among other metadata, in conjunction with SPCS inference. This can be applied at once to all models currently in the schema or to models that may be created in the future.

steps.title: alias specification
steps.body: Set the alias using `ALTER MODEL model_name VERSION v SET ALIAS = name` and disable it with `UNSET ALIAS`. An alias is a convenient nickname that can be easily reassigned and can be used in most places where a version name is expected.

steps.title: Rules of alias
steps.body: In one version, only one alias can be attached. The alias name must be unique within the model and cannot overlap with system aliases. `DEFAULT` refers to the base version, `FIRST` refers to the oldest version, and `LAST` refers to the most recent version.

steps.title: Basic version
steps.body: The `ALTER MODEL` `DEFAULT_VERSION` option defines the default version used when directly calling a method from a model. The system alias `DEFAULT` refers to this default version. Please distinguish between the alias and the default version, as their purposes are different.

screens.outro: Having verified the object structure, we'll now apply an example where model calls are permitted only to specific teams.

screens.title: Explanation example: Allow model calls only to specific teams
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of configuring the AI_COMPLETE to be called only by the customer support team. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: Only the customer support team will generate summaries using `AI_COMPLETE`, preventing other teams from making calls. This case involves an existing account that still has the legacy allow list `All` in place.

steps.title: Step 1: Basic Open and Close
steps.body: Revoke PUBLIC's `USE AI FUNCTIONS` to close the default grant. If not revoked, subsequent grants will be meaningless because all users can already access it.

steps.title: Step 2: Granting Function Permissions
steps.body: Grant the customer support role the specific `USE AI FUNCTION AI_COMPLETE` privilege and the required database roles. This individual privilege does not grant access to other AI functions.

steps.title: Step 3: Model Access Summary
steps.body: The allowed model grants access only to the customer support role via RBAC, with the allowed list set to `None`. If the allowed list is set to `All`, the marketing role would also be able to access the model, so it must be changed.

steps.title: Step 4: Verification via two roles
steps.body: Verification calls both the customer support role and the marketing role to confirm the difference. When called by ACCOUNTADMIN, it always succeeds, thus not verifying the role. It is also forgotten to disable the auxiliary role.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: In this case, two aspects needed to be closed: function call permissions and model access allowance scope. If only one of these is restricted, calls can still proceed through the other, so both devices must be inspected together.

steps.title: What remains after the change
steps.body: After completing the configuration, it's a good idea to document the changes. Having a list of which roles have which functions and models open enables the team to extend consistently when new members are added or new models are introduced. The SNOWFLAKE.MODELS schema is updated daily with new models, so teams that have granted access to all models should remember that future models will automatically be accessible as well.

screens.outro: With access control lifted, let's now examine an example of specifying the operating version in the registry.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Specifying the Operating Version in the Registry
screens.lead: When you select an item, the instructor's explanation will be displayed. First, think for yourself about how you would handle it, then try it.

items.prompt: After validating the internal classification model v3, how do we promote it to the operational version?
items.answer: Move the `PROD` alias to v3. In sentence form, this is `ALTER MODEL model_name VERSION v3 SET ALIAS = PROD`. If this alias was previously assigned to another version, it must first be removed or migrated. This is because only one version can have the same alias at a time.

items.prompt: How should the calling code be modified?
items.answer: The call code uses aliases instead of version names. This way, the operating version can be updated without modifying the code. If the version name is hardcoded in the code, the task of first replacing it with an alias is required.

items.prompt: What happens when a problem occurs?
items.answer: Reassign `PROD` to the previous version. Since only the alias is moved and the new version is not deleted, rollback is quick, and the problematic version can be used for root cause analysis.

items.prompt: What permissions are granted to the team using this model?
items.answer: Teams using SPCS inference are assigned `READ`, while teams handling only warehouse inference are assigned `USAGE`. The principle is to provide only the necessary amount, and for teams whose internal structure does not need to be viewed, `USAGE` is appropriate. While it is possible to assign schemas to both existing and future models at once, one must keep in mind that future models will also be automatically enabled.

items.prompt: In this scenario, what is the first risk to inspect?
items.answer: If the permission to move aliases is broad, anyone could potentially change the operating version. It is safer to grant alias movement permissions only to roles that own the model, and to provide read and usage permissions only to the teams that use it. It is better to assign model invocation permissions and operating version change permissions to different individuals.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the core of the lesson in one go.

paragraphs: In Snowflake, model invocations are also controlled as permission objects. To use AI functions, both account permissions and database roles are required, and by default, public has permissions allowing anyone to invoke them.

The scope of callable models is defined by an allow list and RBAC. Since these two are combined with an OR condition, to use RBAC alone, the allow list must be set to `None`. ACCOUNTADMIN cannot verify restrictions.

The models I registered are managed for operational references using versions and aliases in the Model Registry, and I define usage scopes with permissions `USAGE` and `READ`. Once the initial question is answered, to block model invocations, both function permissions and model allowed scopes must be revoked.

The order to verify during design is as follows: first, close the default public access; next, grant function permissions and database roles to the required roles; finally, organize model access scopes using RBAC. Always perform verification using a role other than ACCOUNTADMIN.

glossary.def: This is an account-level permission that allows calling AI functions. It is initially granted to PUBLIC.
This parameter specifies which models can be called from a account. It accepts one of the following values: All, None, or one of the model name lists.
This is a feature in Snowflake that manages models and versions, metadata as schema-level objects.
A movable name attached to a model version. One per version, and DEFAULT, FIRST, LAST are system aliases.
This is an SQL statement used to modify basic versions, aliases, tags, comments, etc. of a model.

misconceptions.myth: AI functions are used only by active teams.
misconceptions.fact: In the basic settings, everyone has public permission and can use it. Access must be restricted.

misconceptions.myth: The allow list and RBAC operate only one at a time.
misconceptions.fact: Together, access is possible as long as one side permits.

misconceptions.myth: You can verify whether the restriction is correct by checking with ACCOUNTADMIN.
misconceptions.fact: ACCOUNTADMIN can access without restrictions, so it must be verified against other roles.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: Model calls are also authorization objects.
AI functions require both account permissions and database roles.
The new model access control is designed using RBAC and carries over the previous behavior by verifying the applicability of the existing allow list.
The version and alias of the Model Registry define the operational reference.
closing.reflectionLead: The following question is for your own reflection. Answers will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In our platform, what mechanisms allow model invocations, and what is the default openness status?

title: Snowflake model access controls and Registry

checks.q: I haven't changed the account's basic settings, yet the marketing role can call AI_COMPLETE. What is the most likely reason?
options: ACCOUNTADMIN is automatically promoted to the marketing role.
CORTEX_MODELS_ALLOWLIST is always fixed to All.
Individual function-level permissions are automatically granted to the entire account.
The AI functions are by default assigned to PUBLIC.
checks.explain: AI FUNCTIONS are by default assigned to PUBLIC, allowing all users to use them. After being revoked from PUBLIC, they should be granted exclusively to specific roles to reduce the number of authorized users.

wrong.0: There is no scenario in which a role automatically elevates.
wrong.1: The allowed list is a configurable parameter and not a fixed value.
wrong.2: Individual permissions are created only when explicitly granted. The reason for the default openness is the PUBLIC grant.

checks.intro: You've just learned about the basic permission structure. Select the reason why it's being called even though no settings have been changed. This is an unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The permissions granted by default to PUBLIC are inherited by all roles.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Consider what permissions are commonly applied to all roles without having changed any settings.

checks.q: Pair Snowflake's privileges and settings with their respective meanings.
right: Model permissions for warehouse inference that do not have internal visibility
Parameter to specify the call allowance model at the account level
Model permissions that allow inference and metadata browsing
checks.explain: USAGE is for warehouse inference, while READ allows SPCS inference as well as metadata viewing. The allowed list is an account-level parameter, and DEFAULT, FIRST, LAST are system aliases.
checks.intro: Match the privileges and settings of Snowflake with their meanings. Scores are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: All permissions and settings have been properly linked according to their meaning.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs do not match. Please distinguish between warehouse inference permissions, SPCS inference permissions, parameters, and system aliases.

checks.q: In an account where the legacy allowed list is still in effect, the list is set to All, and under RBAC, the model is only opened for the Customer Support role. How does marketing role access to the model work?
options: RBAC is more granular, so the marketing role is disabled.
The list is allowed, so access is granted.
Both methods are combined with AND to allow access only to customer support.
checks.explain: Both methods can be used together, allowing access through either one. To restrict access using only RBAC, the allow list must be set to None.

wrong.0: Greater specificity does not imply priority and is instead combined with OR.
wrong.2: The combination method is OR, not AND.
wrong.3: ACCOUNTADMIN can access all models, but this is not a reason to block other roles.

checks.intro: Consider the outcome when both methods are applied. An unrecorded self-assessment.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The two methods are combined with an OR operation, allowing access if either one is permitted.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Check the bonding configuration again. The key point is how the result behaves when one side is blocked and the other side is left open.
